title: Shridhar's feast and the all-night jagran
hook: a little girl tells a poor man to feed the whole village, and a Punjabi lane stays up all night for her
carry: the mother feeds everyone who comes
tomorrow: why throw sesame into a winter fire?

segments.voice: Yesterday, if the mind is pure, the ganga is here: Ravidas at his bench, and the Ganga in a cobbler's bowl.

In the hills of Jammu, the story goes, lived a poor man named Shridhar who loved the Goddess. One day a little girl came to him and said: hold a feast, a bhandara, and invite the whole village. Shridhar looked at his kitchen. He could barely feed himself. But he went door to door anyway, and the whole village came, far more people than his little house could hold. Today, what the girl did next, and why a Punjabi family still stays up all night for her.
screen: `A POOR MAN, A LITTLE GIRL.` → `FEED THE WHOLE VILLAGE.` → `HE COULD BARELY FEED HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: As the shrine's legend tells it, the girl served everyone herself, and every guest ate. One guest, a proud yogi named Bhairon, demanded meat and wine, and when she refused, he tried to grab her. She slipped away up the Trikuta mountain. Shridhar was heartbroken, until, the story says, she came to him in a dream and showed him her cave. That cave is Vaishno Devi, one of India's most visited shrines, where pilgrims climb day and night calling Jai Mata Di: victory to the Mother. Here's the teaching inside the story. In devotion to the Goddess, she is Mata, Mother: the one who feeds, and who comes in the smallest form, a little girl, to a man with nothing. That's why at Navratri many families wash the feet of young girls and feed them as the Goddess. And it's why a Punjabi family whose prayer was answered, a baby born, an illness passed, holds a jagran: a waking, a vigil. A picture of the Mother goes up in a tent in the lane. The lamp before her, the jyot, burns till dawn. Singers lead bhents, songs offered to her, and kids fall asleep on laps. At dawn comes prasad, food offered to her and then shared. And the whole lane is invited, like Shridhar's village. You don't thank the Mother and keep the blessing to yourself. What she gives, you set before her, then share with everyone who comes.
screen: `SHRIDHAR'S FEAST: EVERY GUEST ATE` · `THE CAVE AT VAISHNO DEVI` · `MATA: THE MOTHER WHO FEEDS` · `JAGRAN: A NIGHT AWAKE IN THANKS` · then, large: `THE WHOLE LANE IS INVITED.`

segments.voice: Let the tent's words ride on your breath. If you pray, say Jai Mata Di softly on each out-breath, and on each in-breath bring to mind one thing that came to you this year as a gift. If you don't pray, simply name the gifts, one per breath, and for each one, think of someone you could share it with.
Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, the jagran: a night awake for the Mother, with the whole lane invited, the way Shridhar invited his village. Today's word.
Your line: the mother feeds everyone who comes. A lamp kept lit, and a lane kept company, until dawn. Rest well.

howItsDone: Punjabi Hindu families hold a jagran, or jagrata, for Mata, often in thanks for a blessing: singers lead devotional songs through the night before a lit jyot, the neighbors are invited, and prasad is shared at dawn.

chat.meaning: In the Vaishno Devi legend the Goddess, as a little girl, fed Shridhar's whole village. A jagran thanks the Mother the same way: songs all night, and prasad shared with everyone who comes.
